title: NOCTI Biotechnology 4275: Safety in the Biotechnology Laboratory - Biotechnology - Emergency showers, eyewash stations
exam: NOCTI Biotechnology 4275: Safety in the Biotechnology Laboratory
subject: Biotechnology

questions.q: A technician accidentally splashes a dilute basic solution ($0.1 \text{ M NaOH}$) into their unprotected eyes. They rapidly run to the plumbed facility eyewash station, turn on the water, and hold their eyelids completely open in the stream. What is the standard, OSHA-mandated minimum duration the technician must continuously flush their eyes?
questions.explain:
According to the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) Z358.1, which is heavily enforced by OSHA, emergency eyewash stations and safety showers must be capable of providing a massive, uninterrupted flow of tepid flushing fluid for a minimum of **15 continuous minutes**. 

Flushing for less than 15 minutes significantly increases the risk that trace amounts of the chemical (especially tissue-destroying bases like NaOH) remain trapped deep in the mucous membranes of the eye, continuing to cause permanent thermal and chemical burns.

questions.q: A large volume of a highly corrosive acid accidentally spills off a bench, splashing directly onto a technician's chest and completely soaking through their cotton lab coat into their underlying clothing. The technician immediately steps under the laboratory's emergency safety shower and pulls the overhead activation handle. What is the critical next step the technician must take while standing under the flowing water?
options: Wait patiently for the flowing water to chemically neutralize the acid before attempting to touch or remove any clothing.
Actively and rapidly remove all contaminated clothing, including the lab coat, shirt, and shoes, while the massive volume of water continues to flush the skin.
Use a specialized chemical absorbent spill pillow to physically scrub the acid off the fabric while remaining under the water.
Turn off the water after exactly 30 seconds to prevent environmental runoff from flooding the laboratory floor, then gently undress.
questions.explain:
During a massive chemical exposure, contaminated clothing essentially acts as a chemical sponge, pressing the burning agent tightly against the skin. 

The safety shower exists to physically wash the chemical off the body (dilution), but it cannot penetrate heavily soaked clothing quickly enough to stop the burn. The operator must **strip off all contaminated clothing** as rapidly as possible while standing directly under the deluge of the running shower. Privacy is completely secondary to preventing a severe chemical burn.

questions.q: According to strict safety compliance guidelines (such as ANSI Z358.1), plumbed emergency eyewash stations must be mechanically activated and visually inspected by laboratory personnel on a rigid routine schedule. What is the required frequency for this preventative testing, and what is its primary operational purpose?
options: Annually; to test the entire laboratory building's maximum water pressure limits and structural pipe integrity.
Monthly; to mechanically clear the connected sink drain trap of accidentally dropped pipettes and glassware.
Weekly; to verify instant mechanical operation and to physically flush out stagnant water, rust, and potentially infectious microbial buildup from the feed pipes.
Daily; to ensure the internal water temperature rapidly reaches a sterilizing threshold of $100^\circ\text{C}$ before use.
questions.explain:
Plumbed eyewash stations must be flushed **weekly**. 

Because they are rarely used during normal operations, the "dead leg" pipes feeding the station collect stagnant water. This stagnation promotes the growth of dangerous microbes (like *Acanthamoeba* or *Legionella*), as well as the accumulation of sediment and rust. Flushing the station weekly for 1-3 minutes ensures that if a technician splashes acid in their eyes, they are flushing their open wounds with clean water, not a stagnant pool of infectious bacteria.

questions.q: An aging piece of electrical equipment in the laboratory violently short-circuits, sparking an aggressive electrical fire inside its internal wiring. Which strict classification of fire extinguisher is specifically rated, required, and safe to use when combating an actively energized electrical fire?
options: Class C (Carbon Dioxide or Dry Chemical)
Class D (Dry Powder for Combustible Metals)
questions.explain:
Using the wrong fire extinguisher can be fatal. 

Shooting pressurized water (Class A) or wet foam (Class B) onto an energized electrical fire will conduct the current directly back up the stream of water, severely electrocuting the user. **Class C** extinguishers (often filled with non-conductive Carbon Dioxide or inert dry chemicals) are specifically formulated to smother electrical fires without conducting lethal currents back to the operator.
